"Raise" always means you are causing something to go higher, increase, or come into being. You are the one doing it. Something else is receiving your action.

This is the soul of the word. Every meaning of "raise" you will ever encounter is a version of this idea — either literally (physically lifting) or figuratively (causing something to grow, intensify, or appear).
One Grammar Rule You Must Know

"Raise" always needs an object — meaning, you always raise something. You cannot just "raise." You raise your hand. You raise prices. You raise a child.

This is what separates "raise" from "rise." "Rise" happens on its own — the sun rises, prices rise. But with "raise," you are the cause. You are doing it to something.

Think of it this way:

  • The bread rises on its own. → No one is causing it.
  • The baker raises the temperature. → The baker is causing the change.

Keep this rule in mind as you read the rest of this guide.
All the Meanings, One by One

1. To Move Something Physically Upward

This is the most literal meaning. You lift something from a lower position to a higher one.

  • She raised the window blind to let in sunlight.
  • He raised his arm to ask a question in class.
  • The workers raised the flag on the pole.
  • The crane raised the heavy steel beam.

Anything you physically lift or pull upward — you "raise" it.

2. To Increase an Amount, Level, or Degree

Here, "raise" means to make something greater — a number, a price, a temperature, a standard.

  • The company raised the employees' salaries.
  • The government raised taxes this year.
  • He turned the dial to raise the volume.
  • The teacher raised her expectations for the class.
  • Scientists raised the temperature in the experiment.

Notice how in all these cases, something goes up — not in space, but in value or intensity.

3. To Bring Up and Nurture a Child, Animal, or Crop

When you raise a living thing, you take care of it from an early stage of life and help it grow to maturity.

  • Her grandparents raised her after her parents passed away.
  • They raise chickens and goats on their farm.
  • Farmers in this region raise wheat and rice.
  • He was raised in a small village in the mountains. (This means he grew up there, under someone's care.)

Notice that you can "raise" children, animals, and even plants/crops. In all cases, the idea is the same: you are responsible for their growth and survival over a long period.

4. To Bring Up a Topic, Question, or Issue in a Conversation

When you "raise" something in conversation, you bring it to people's attention — you introduce it for others to notice or discuss.

  • She raised an important question during the meeting.
  • Nobody raised any objections to the plan.
  • He raised his concerns about the safety of the building.
  • The journalist raised the issue of corruption.
  • The report raised doubts about the company's honesty.

Think of it as lifting a topic up into the conversation — making it visible, just like lifting something off the floor so everyone can see it.

5. To Collect or Gather Money, Support, or People

When you raise funds, an army, or support, you are gathering resources — bringing them together from different places so that the total grows.

  • The charity raised five million rupees for flood victims.
  • The startup raised funds from investors.
  • The king raised an army to defend the kingdom.
  • They raised enough support to win the election.

The idea is the same — you are causing a number or a group to grow and increase.

6. To Cause a Feeling, Reaction, or Situation to Appear

"Raise" can also mean to produce or trigger something — often a feeling, a reaction, or a situation that wasn't there before.

  • The news raised everyone's hopes.
  • The horror movie raised her anxiety.
  • His rude comment raised eyebrows in the room. (This means people were surprised or disapproving.)
  • The politician's speech raised the crowd's spirits.
  • Her unusual behavior raised suspicion among her colleagues.

Here, you are not lifting a physical thing. You are causing something — a feeling or a reaction — to come into existence or to intensify.

7. To Make Your Voice Louder

When you raise your voice, you speak more loudly. Often this implies anger or urgency, though not always.

  • Please do not raise your voice at me.
  • She had to raise her voice to be heard over the noise.
  • He never raises his voice, even when he's frustrated.

8. To Bring Up Something to a Higher Level or Status

"Raise" can mean to promote, elevate, or upgrade something — in rank, status, importance, or quality.

  • The company raised him to the position of manager.
  • The government plans to raise the standard of public schools.
  • This discovery raised the profile of the young scientist.

9. To Formally End a Restriction or Siege

In formal or official language, "raise" can mean to lift a ban, a blockade, a siege, or sanctions — meaning to end or remove them.

  • The government raised the ban on imports.
  • After months, the army finally raised the siege of the city.
  • The UN voted to raise the sanctions on the country.

Here, "raise" means to "lift" a restriction — as if removing something that was weighing something else down.

10. Specific Uses You Will Encounter

In card games (like poker):
To raise means to increase the bet above what the previous player put in.

  • He raised the bet to a thousand rupees.

To raise a toast:
When people lift their glasses before drinking to honor someone, this is called raising a toast.

  • He raised a toast to the bride and groom.

To raise the alarm:
To alert people about a danger or problem.

  • She raised the alarm when she smelled smoke in the building.

In mathematics:
To raise a number to a power means to multiply it by itself that many times.

  • Two raised to the power of three equals eight. (2³ = 8)

To raise the dead (literary/religious):
To bring someone back to life. Also used figuratively to mean reviving something that had ended or died out.

  • The story says the prophet could raise the dead.
  • She raised the old tradition from obscurity.

These are fixed expressions you will hear very often. Knowing them will save you a lot of confusion.

  • Raise the bar — to set a higher standard for quality or performance.
    "Their new product really raised the bar for the industry."
  • Raise hell / raise a ruckus — to cause trouble, argue loudly, or protest.
    "He raised hell when his order was wrong."
  • Raise the stakes — to make something more important, risky, or competitive.
    "Investing your savings really raises the stakes."
  • Raise awareness — to make people more conscious of an issue.
    "The campaign was designed to raise awareness about mental health."
  • Raise a red flag — to signal a warning or concern.
    "The missing documents raised a red flag for the auditors."
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

You almost never need to guess. The word that comes after "raise" tells you everything:

  • Raise + hand/flag/arm/curtain → physical upward movement
  • Raise + salary/price/tax/temperature → increase in amount
  • Raise + child/animals/crops → nurturing and growing
  • Raise + question/issue/concern/objection → bringing something into discussion
  • Raise + money/funds/army → gathering resources
  • Raise + hopes/spirits/doubts/suspicion → causing a feeling or reaction
  • Raise + voice → speaking more loudly
  • Raise + ban/siege/sanctions → formally ending a restriction

Every single meaning of "raise" — whether you're lifting a box, increasing a price, nurturing a child, or starting a conversation about a problem — is a variation of the same idea:

You are causing something to go up, grow, increase, or come into existence.

You are always the agent. You are always the cause. And something else is always moving upward or becoming more because of you.

Master this central idea, and every use of "raise" — even ones you encounter for the first time — will make perfect sense.
